scenes.title: Welcome

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Learn a topic with your assistant
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Answer yourself. The assistant passes your words on and must not answer, choose or rate for you.

scenes.markdown:
This lesson ships with Studium and takes about ten minutes. It shows how Studium works by making you use it: each mechanism is explained on the step where you meet it.

**Look at the top of the screen first.** The notice there says who wrote this lesson and what is assessed. It is true of this lesson too: an AI agent drafted it from Studium's own documentation, and no teacher has checked it yet. In the VS Code pane the notice is the banner above the step; in a chat, your assistant shows it on the first screen.

**You answer, the assistant relays.** Studium asks the questions and keeps the answer keys. When you play through an assistant (Copilot, Claude Code, Codex or another), it shows each step as Studium wrote it, waits for your answer and passes your own words on. It must never answer, choose or rate for you.

Continue when you are ready.

scenes.title: Who answers

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Learn a topic with your assistant
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Answer yourself. The assistant passes your words on and must not answer, choose or rate for you.

scenes.question:
You play this lesson through an assistant. Who should give the answer to this question?

Before you answer, you may say how confident you are, from 0 (not confident) to 4 (very confident): in the VS Code pane, tap a number in the row under the choices; in a chat, say it with your answer, for example "A, confidence 3", and your assistant can pass it on. It is optional. Studium compares that confidence with what your answers show.

choices.text: You: the assistant shows the step and passes your own words on
The assistant, since it can read the whole lesson
Studium, which picks the most likely answer for you

scenes.feedback_correct: Right. Studium keeps the keys and the assistant only relays: your answer, in your words.
scenes.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Think about whose knowledge the lesson is measuring.
hints: Studium measures what you know, not what the assistant knows.

scenes.title: A course is a graph

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — How Studium works
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: The Learning Workflow Graph (LWG) has two kinds of nodes, *concepts* and *tasks*, and typed edges

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — How Studium works
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: When a prerequisite is missing, the session can route the learner to it first and then return.

scenes.markdown:
A Studium lesson is more than a list of screens. Each step, a *scene*, is tied to one or more **concepts**, and the concepts are linked in a typed graph, the Learning Workflow Graph: an edge such as `prerequisite_for` says that one idea must be in place before another.

This lesson has five concepts. Two links matter here: *Who holds the key* needs *A course is a graph* first, and *Spaced reviews* needs *Who holds the key*.

The graph helps decide what comes next. When you reach a concept whose prerequisite is still missing, the lesson can make a **detour** to a question on that prerequisite, then come back. After two errors in a row on the same concept, it replays the step. That is remediation.

**Try it:** open the concept map. In the VS Code pane, press **Concept map** under the step; in a chat, ask "where am I?". Each concept shows its state: acquired, to review, in progress, seen but not assessed yet, or upcoming.

scenes.title: When a prerequisite is missing

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — How Studium works
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: When a prerequisite is missing, the session can route the learner to it first and then return.

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Student guide
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: A detour sends you to a prerequisite and then back.

scenes.question:
In this lesson, *Who holds the key* needs *A course is a graph*. What can happen if you reach it while *A course is a graph* is still missing?

Stuck? Ask for a **hint**: the **Hint** button in the pane, or "a hint, please" in a chat. A right answer given after a hint counts a little less toward your mastery, and comes back sooner for review.

choices.text: The lesson makes a detour to a question on the missing prerequisite, then comes back
Nothing: the steps always follow the same order, whatever you answer
The lesson stops until a teacher unlocks the concept

scenes.feedback_correct: Yes. The graph is part of the lesson file, so a teacher can read and correct it, and the lesson uses it to choose the next step.
scenes.feedback_incorrect: Not this one. Open the concept map and look at what each concept needs first.
hints: Read the third paragraph of the previous step again.
The concept map says, for each concept, what it needs first.

scenes.title: Who holds the key

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Honesty and provenance
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Studium tells the learner who wrote each answer key, whether anything actually assessed their answer, and whether a teacher validated the lesson.

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Honesty and provenance
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: An exact quote proves a textual link, not that the item uses it correctly.

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Learn a topic with your assistant
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: every quotation must match a passage character for character

scenes.markdown:
Every answer is assessed by whoever holds its key, and Studium tells you who that is.

- A **quiz** is checked against the key its author wrote. Here the author is an AI agent; in the pane, the line over the verdict says so: "Assessed by the AI-drafted key — check it against the cited passage".
- A **written answer** (an explanation, a comparison) is assessed only by a judge model, when one is configured. Without one, Studium does not pretend: it shows you a reference and you compare yourself. It never counts keywords.
- Only assessed answers move your **mastery**.

**Sources.** Each question of this lesson cites a passage of Studium's documentation. Studium refused to write the lesson until every quotation matched its passage character for character. The passages appear after you answer, when you leave the step, so they never give the answer away. An exact quote proves a textual link, not that the question uses it well: if a key looks wrong to you, say so.

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Honesty and provenance
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: The approval record is the only source of the validated status.

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Honesty and provenance
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Demo lesson shipped with Studium, drafted by an AI agent from Studium's documentation, not checked by a teacher

scenes.question: Who wrote the key that checks your answers to the questions of this lesson?

choices.text: An AI agent, from Studium's documentation; no teacher has checked it yet
A teacher, who validated the lesson
Nobody: Studium compares your words with a list of keywords

scenes.feedback_correct: Right, and the notice at the top said so. A lesson reads as validated only when a teacher's approval record matches its exact file.
scenes.feedback_incorrect: Not this one. Look at the notice at the top of the lesson again.
hints: The notice at the top of the lesson names who drafted it.

scenes.title: Why not count keywords

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Honesty and provenance
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Matching authored cue words anywhere in an answer measures vocabulary, not understanding: measured against a teacher on a real lesson, it inverted 11 answers out of 12.

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Honesty and provenance
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Without a judge, the feedback shows the reference to compare with and states no count.

scenes.prompt:
In two or three sentences of your own: why does Studium not score a written answer by counting the expected words, and what does it do instead when no judge model is configured?

After you send it, you will see the key points and a model answer. Compare them with what you wrote, then rate how well you recalled it: again, hard, good or easy.

key_points.text: Finding the expected words measures vocabulary, not understanding
Without a judge, the answer is not assessed: you compare it with a reference
Your recall rating schedules your reviews and never changes your mastery

scenes.model_explanation: Finding the expected words in an answer shows that you know the vocabulary, not that you understood: on a real lesson, checked against a teacher, keyword scoring inverted 11 answers out of 12. So without a judge model Studium assesses nothing: it shows the key points and a model answer, you compare yourself and rate your recall. That rating only sets the date of your next review; it never changes your mastery.

scenes.title: Reviews over days

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Review over time
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Yes: wrong reads as "again", right after a hint as "hard", right as "good"

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Review over time
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: It is never treated as proof that you know the concept

scenes.markdown:
Studium brings a concept back when you are about to forget it. For each concept it keeps a memory model, FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler), that estimates how likely you are to recall it now.

- A quiz answer schedules a review by itself: wrong reads as "again", right after a hint as "hard", right as "good".
- After a written answer no judge assessed, **your recall rating** sets the next review. It is your own judgement, so it never changes your mastery.
- A reading step or a confidence check schedules nothing.

**Where reviews show up afterwards.** The last screen of this lesson gives your next review date. Later, in VS Code, the status bar counts what is waiting ("Studium · 2 to review") and the sidebar has a Reviews entry. With an assistant, ask "What should I study with Studium today?": it reads your study plan, then plays the reviews due across all your lessons.

scenes.title: What your rating changes

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Honesty and provenance
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: The rating schedules the next review (FSRS) for every concept of the rated scene and never moves mastery.

scenes.question: After a written answer no judge assessed, you rate your recall "good". What does that change?

choices.text: Only when the concept comes back for review
Your mastery of the concept goes up
Both your mastery and the date of your next review

scenes.feedback_correct: Yes. Your rating is your own judgement: it schedules, it does not measure.
scenes.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Ask yourself whether a rating you give yourself can count as evidence of what you know.
hints: Reread what the rating screen said under "Rate your recall".

scenes.title: Where your data lives

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Privacy and limits
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: That does not mean everything stays local: an assistant connected to a remote model sends what it reads to its provider.

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Privacy and limits
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Inside the data folder, each learner has a folder named by a pseudonym, never by their id

scenes.markdown:
Studium keeps your progress on your own machine.

- With an assistant, the lessons it builds for you go to `~/.studium/library` and your progress to `~/.studium/data`, in folders named by a pseudonym, never by your id. The VS Code extension keeps its own progress in VS Code's storage.
- Class telemetry is off unless you opt in.
- **What leaves your machine** is what your assistant reads: if it runs on a remote model, the steps it shows and the answers it relays go to that model's provider, under the provider's terms. Playing in the VS Code pane needs no AI account.
- To erase your progress, ask your assistant to forget your data, or run **Studium: Forget my data** in VS Code.

This lesson ships with Studium, inside the VS Code extension and the npm package. It stays apart from your library: it never replaces a lesson of yours. When you are done, build a lesson from your own sources: tell your assistant "I want to learn … with Studium".

scenes.title: What leaves your machine

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Privacy and limits
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: That does not mean everything stays local: an assistant connected to a remote model sends what it reads to its provider.

scenes.question: You play this lesson through an assistant that runs on a remote model. What leaves your machine?

choices.text: What the assistant reads and relays, sent to its model provider
Nothing at all: everything stays on your machine
Your progress, sent to a Studium server

scenes.feedback_correct: Right. Studium keeps its state on your machine; the assistant's provider sees what the assistant reads. Choose an assistant whose terms suit you.
scenes.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Think about the assistant itself, not only Studium.
hints: Where does your assistant's model run?

scenes.title: Reading the map

bibliographic_refs.title: Studium documentation — Concept map
bibliographic_refs.excerpt: Each concept says its state in words and what it needs first.

scenes.question:
One more question on the graph of this lesson. Which concept had to be in place before *Spaced reviews*?

The concept map answers it: each concept says what it needs first.

choices.text: Who holds the key, and where it comes from

scenes.feedback_correct: Yes. You can read the whole graph of a lesson in its concept map, and a teacher can read and correct it in the lesson file.
scenes.feedback_incorrect: Not this one. Open the concept map and look at what *Spaced reviews* needs first.
hints: Open the concept map: each concept lists what it needs first.
